## How to catch a neutrino? {#how-to-catch}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
{{< nh-video icecube-first-pev variant="web-en" class="slide-video media-height-lg" style="--media-max-height: 560px;" controls=true muted=true playsinline=true preload="metadata" poster="media/films/icecube_build_en.jpg" aria-label="86 holes are melted 2.5 km into the ice under the IceCube Laboratory, 5160 light sensors appear, and the PeV cascades Bert, Ernie and Big Bird each light hundreds of sensors from inside the detector." >}}

::: {.media-caption}
Sensor positions: IceCube geometry · light pattern modelled · Bert and Ernie:
[IceCube 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.5356) · Big Bird: [IceCube 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.5303), position illustrative
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**We will need:**

- **A huge transparent target:** water or ice.
- **Darkness:** the sensors catch single photons.
- **Depth:** kilometres of water or ice stop the muons from cosmic rays.
- **The Earth as a shield:** from below, through the whole Earth, only neutrinos get through.
- **A lattice of light sensors** spaced tens of metres apart.
:::
:::::

## Cherenkov light {#cherenkov}

:::::: {.panel-tabset}

### The film

{{< nh-video cherenkov-radiation variant="film-dipoles-en" class="slide-video media-height-lg" style="--media-max-height: 590px;" controls=true muted=true playsinline=true preload="metadata" poster="media/films/cherenkov_dipoles_en.jpg" aria-label="A charge polarises the molecules of water into small dipoles. Around a slow charge the dipoles are symmetric and their fields cancel. A fast charge leaves the dipoles behind; each piece of the track sends out a wavelet, the wavelets add up only along a common front, and light goes perpendicular to it at the angle cos theta = 1/(n beta). Turned about the track, the front is a cone." >}}

::: {.media-caption}
Gold: charge · dots: molecules · bars: induced dipoles (− blue, + red) · blue circles: wavelets · white: common front · cyan: light · schematic after J. V. Jelley, *Čerenkov Radiation and Its Applications* (1958), §1.2
:::

### Why a cone?

- The particle moves in water faster than light does in water: $v > c/n$.
- It overtakes its own waves, and they add up into a common front, a cone.
- In the same way a boat leaves a wedge of waves behind it, and a supersonic aircraft a shock wave.
- Light goes across this front at the angle $\theta_C$, about $41^\circ$ in water:

$$
\cos\theta_C=\frac{1}{n\beta}.
$$

```{=html}
<div data-nerpa="dash" class="fragment" data-from="left" data-size="260" data-duration="3.4" style="left: 0; right: 0; top: 70%; height: 24%;"></div>
```

## One photon, a measurable signal {#photomultiplier}

:::::: {.panel-tabset}

### Photomultiplier

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
{{< nh-video pmt-juno variant="web-en" class="slide-video media-height-lg" style="--media-max-height: 680px;" controls=true muted=true playsinline=true preload="metadata" poster="media/films/pmt_juno_en.jpg" aria-label="A 20-inch photomultiplier: one photon releases a photoelectron from the photocathode, ten dynodes multiply the charge, and the anode collects an electrical pulse." >}}
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
- A photon knocks one electron out of a thin photocathode.
- The electric field accelerates it towards the first dynode.
- Each impact on a dynode knocks out several new electrons.
- After ten dynodes, the anode collects an electrical pulse.

::: {.media-caption}
20-inch photomultiplier R12860 (Hamamatsu), as in [JUNO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.08629) · bulb after the Hamamatsu drawing, internal electrodes reconstructed, trajectories calculated in a 3D field
:::
:::
:::::

## Which event points better back to its source? {#quiz-track-shower-answer}

:::: {.quiz-slide}
::: {.quiz-options .two-options}

::: {.quiz-option .correct}
**A.** A track: a muon crosses the detector
:::

::: {.quiz-option .wrong}
**B.** A shower: a ball of light inside the detector
:::
